blocks.x: You can go ahead, it's running now.
Okay, it's going now. I guess the first thing we should get is your right name.

Well, I was christened James Preston MacDonald. But you see, my mother and father separated, about three years old. So my mother remarried Charles Jackson, he was a brick major. And so I take the name of Jackson, I used my middle name Preston. His name was Charles Jackson. Yeah.
I noticed Preston J. Jackson when you signed it.

Yeah, I used that J because James was my first name. So it just twisted around a bit, Preston J. I'm better known, it's only the people that I attended school with know me back down. But I'm known professionally as Preston Jackson.
And where were you born and when?
I was born in 1902, up on Hillary Street. I don't remember the number, I heard my mother say, but that's up in Carrollton.
On Hillary?
Yeah.
I know exactly where that is. How far from the river?
I really don't know.
You don't remember that? No, I was small. When you were a baby there?

Yeah, I was a baby, you know. And I moved from up there, and in fact my parents did. They moved from there on to Palmer's Avenue. And so I must have been about, maybe around six years old, something like that. That's where I first saw Roy Palmer.
That was his street, huh?
Yeah, he lived right on Palmer's Avenue. Yeah.
What was the Cross Street? Do you remember? 100th Park?
I don't remember what the Cross Street is now, but let's see. I'll try to get as close as possible. That would be up there with the Fred. And then coming back from Fred would be what the...
Let's see, Robertson?
Yeah, it's Lou. Clara? It would be somewhere around Clara. Yeah, around Clara.
Clara Street, yeah. You weren't far from the back part of Tulane University where we are? Not too far away. Yeah. No. Because I guess they didn't have the...
Not too far away from Audubon Park either.
Yeah.
Not too far away, you know.
Yeah.
It wasn't a few blocks either, but it was in walking distance.
Yeah. What's your day of birth and month of birth?
January the 3rd, 1902.
Oh, like the 1902.
Yeah.
Did you have any musicians in your family?
Not as I know of it. My mother used to sing, I'd say, very well in the choir, you know, until she began to have trouble. Then she just continued it. But otherwise, I don't know of any in the family.
You didn't know any great uncles or anything like that?

I knew my uncle and my mother was a brother, but we had a great uncle. He moved years before that and lived in Boston, Massachusetts. But we lost track of it. I lost track of a lot of my folks. I have people here, but I don't know where they are now. I'm trying to locate some of them now before I leave.
The one who lived in Boston, did he go to music school or play in Michigan?
Well, he was supposed to be a professor. Yeah. So she told me. I never did see him or meet him.
Didn't know his name or anything?
No. She told me, but I'd forgotten.
Well, what about before you went to school? Did you hear any music?

Yeah. Well, sometime my mother would have a fish fry and she was engaged with Roy Palmer. He had a friend that played a mountain. Later on you know Roy Palmer played baritone, cornet, trombone, a lot of instruments. He was a pretty good teacher. He taught a lot of people around Chicago, including myself and Lionel Hampton and Oscar Bunny Young, who I later played with at the Wisconsin Roof for about six years. And McKinley Thomas and Baritone, we had a band around there, including the singing brothers, Homer and Al Simeon. And in this band was, in time, it was Natty Dominic, you know. We played, we were close together like most of New Orleans musicians in Chicago. It was kind of cliquish, you know. Just like Joe and Manuel and Freddie. Every time Joe Oliver wanted Trump to play, I called him to play, he sent him to New Orleans and that one, you know. And so that's what they would do. And they stuck together for quite a while. And until they began to have internal strife, I say, you know. They began to disagree with one another. That was the beginning of Joe Oliver's great band. Some kind of disagreement concerning recordings. Joe used to record under assumed names sometimes, you know. And so I heard that Joe, he changed. He used Eddie Atkinson in the place of Dufres, and he used Jimmy Noon in the place of Jam, Johnny Dodge.

Where was Eddie Atkinson from? New Orleans. I never heard of him down here. Oh, I've seen his greatest, he's buried out by Ron Wagamahema. Did he play with bass down here? Yeah, I think so, but not in early years. In early years.
Well, I saw his picture in his family, family jazz album. Yeah, yeah. And in the uniform of brass band, you know. Yeah, the whole thing. That was a long time before he came to Chicago.
He came to Chicago in the 20s, huh?
Oh, yeah, he must have.
Before that.
Yeah, before that.
Yeah. I'm trying to think, because.

Yeah, Eddie Atkinson is a very good musician. He played mostly in theaters, you know. He played in the Grand Theater for years. Dave Peyton, and he later on with Dave Peyton was at the Regal Theater. He played, I'd taken his place at the Regal Theater. That was before the Vitaphone, you know. We had to play the music for the pictures, fanfare, and then the stage presentation, you know.
Well, back to Roy Palmer and your fish fries. What instrument did he play at the fish fries? You said everything like that.
Bass violin.
Bass violin, and he had a mandolin.
Yeah, a mandolin.
And what would they play, do you know?

Well, they was playing jazz music. Yeah, they was playing jazz music. I guess that's all they knew. That was the main thing. It's always been one of the main things in New Orleans, because there are other bands that play the quadrilles and things like that, you know. But that jazz music, ever since I've been knowing myself I've been hearing it. And so Roy was playing baritone, I saw him in a parade playing baritone and trombone.
Well, what went on at the fish fry? How did that work?
Well, she was selling fish. That's it. Selling fish.
How would the people know whether there was going to be a fish fry in the neighborhood?

Well, there would always be a lantern that would have a stick attached to the house. And on the very end, not too far so it would fall off, was this red lantern. So people would see that in the neighborhood and they knew that they would sell the fish. It was mostly on the side of this.
I often wondered how people would know about it. Yes. They didn't do any advertising for it.
Well, that was the advertisement, the red lantern.
I mean the band didn't go there.
Oh no, oh no, no.
They didn't serenade a stroller.
No, no. That wasn't necessary. It wasn't like later on when they, like a picnic or a dancer would have these bands go around and advertise, mostly on a Sunday, you know.
Well, as you grew on in years, did you hear any more music?

Oh yeah, I, in spite of me hearing this music, I used to say, the second line just like the rest of the kids. We used to try sometime way away from home, you know, out of the neighborhood. I remember I, I think it was about the 30th of May and some friends of mine and I, we, we came all the way down to French Bar Town and the boys got behind us and ran us all the way to the podgers and ramparts, you know. And so I always did love music. I used to do a lot of whistling. I still do. And so, but I didn't have no idea that I'd ever play, play music, you know. And I really started in Chicago. My first instrument was the piano. Well, I, I went, I didn't go any farther and the first waltz and the teacher began to come and I'd be out somewhere else. And so she just continued coming. And so I'd say maybe about a year or two laps, but I continued to go around these different bands, especially the Joao's band. You see, I was fortunate enough to, to have two great trombones. This is, I'd say as teachers, it was Honoré Dutré and Rod Palmer. You see, I would go by the Royal Garden in the evening and sit behind a dutré, we call her Nora. And it was alright with Joao like me. I'd sit there until they would get ready to go. Then we'd leave and we'd go to a place there, 35th and State's and a drug store. We'd get them all to milk a piece with an egg in it, you know, and food around me while I was so then we'd go home. But I always met Jo, but I knew the next day he loved to play pool with. I knew his wife and his daughter. So Dutré was in the neighborhood during World War I. And some kind of way he was found in a magazine where the powder is, you know, I don't know how many hours in there. What he was doing there, dead when he got him out of there. So it affected his breathing. So he was only too glad for me to sit in for him. He'd go back behind and had a curtain, a long curtain. And I'd hear, you know, something he'd be squirting in his throat, you know, or in his nostrils. So I was glad to play too. And it was alright with Jo. So, and Roy, Roy Rumwood, my mother and father. So during that time in Chicago, there were so many jobs and so much, so many musicians, so many things going on. It puts me to mind at Bourbon Street. They had jobs, they had society dances in the mornings. Start at eight o'clock. Such dances they call as the castle walk and some other dances, you know. They played special music for that. Well, Roy was playing with a fellow called Doc Watson at that time. He and Willie Hightower. He's from here too. So I would follow Roy and I'd be sitting right behind him. And that really, they really helped me immensely. And Roy later on, some years later, he discontinued playing, but he continued teaching. But he was some great bands in Chicago, like Hugh Swift, Jeffrey Tavern, orchestra and Dr. Charles Cook's 26th Beast Band at the Harmon's Dreamland. And Doc Watson and other bands. And now Roy, he wasn't, he didn't seem to be in the click from New Orleans. I asked Joe Oliver one day, I said, Joe, why hasn't Roy been playing with you? He said, he just didn't like his playing. But everybody else seemed to like it. And so he just told me. And I never thought about it, spoke to him about it again. I didn't think it was necessary because he told me why. But Dutra, I think, was a great trombone player. And Zoo Robinson used to come through once in a while. Then we had Eddie Vincent too. He was around. And George Field, he was a very good musician. And so it was loaded. They had jobs that started at 12 to 3, short hours. And then we had Charles Huggler, who just died a few weeks ago. He, he must have migrated to Chicago. Chicago must have been in about 1898 or something like that. Because I saw something pertaining to that. And it seemed, from what I gather, he must have, he and Charles Levy, he's another New Orleans musician. Charles Levy went up there in 19, he migrated to Chicago in 1915. And so, Elga had large bands at a place called Riverview. And I had large bands up there during that time. At least 15 pieces, you know, like that. And so, Roy played with the best bands. And there's people right today that say he's the best. Now, we'll take Ory. I saw Ory and I heard Ory before I ever left New Orleans. He and Joe Oliver were together. He played a lot of dances at the National Park Fair in Willow. And I heard Jack Carey and all that bunch. Mutt Carey's brother. And Tee Chambers played at Mrs. Cold's lawn party. I heard all those fellas. And then when I, my parents brought me to Chicago, I heard them again. I heard Lux. They had personnel with Sugar Johnny and, well, Lil Armstrong, who, her name was Harding at that time. Later on, Louie married Lil, you know. Well, our little band, we played for the reception. That was the personnel. Some of the personnel was Oscar Burney Young. I attended school with Oscar Burney Young and Tom Lafond School. I also attended school with Earl Humphrey. I lived just a few blocks from Humphrey at one time. And Joe Rogashio, the pianist. We all attended school together. And there was this drummer, Clifford Snaggs Jones, you might have, he's in his jazz album too. He was left there in German drummer. And this great drummer, the late Sid Catlett, he learned a lot from Snaggs. Snaggs had good rhythm. So this little band, we got together, this is Omi and Simeon, and we played for their reception. Well, getting back to this personnel at the Deluxe was Circa Johnny and they had a Wilman Bro, Roy Palmer, and Baby Hall, which later we called him, his name was Fred. We later called him Tubby Hall, you know. And Bishady played up there. And what the leader was declaring his name was, let's see what his name was, I can't call his name.
Where was he from? He's from New Orleans.
Well, I wouldn't say they all were right from New Orleans, but they're from Louisiana musicians.
Maybe Lafayette or something?
Yeah, some of that, along some of the smaller towns, just like Gore. Gore came from Cut Off or something like that, Louisiana.
Did you ever know Lawrence Dewey?
That's who had the band, Lawrence Dewey.
Oh, I see.

He had the band. Yeah, I couldn't call his name just then. Yeah. And then right across the street was Joe Oliver played over there. Holly Powers did the singing. Joe was doubling, he was doubling at the Pekin. He'd leave the Dreamland and go to Pekin. And then later, at that time now, this Royal Garden, this is when I first saw, I saw Emmanuel Perez here, but this Paul Barber, he was playing drums with this band. And it was Bill Johnson's band, bass player, who lived to be a hundred years old, died, I think it was last year. And so they had Emmanuel and Freddie, Freddie Kevick, Jimmy Newman, and they had Eddie Vincent. And there was a woman playing piano by the name of Lottie Taylor. And Bill Johnson was on the bass. That was the person that was this band. Well, it seemed like they lost out there in time. And the next thing I knew, Joe Oliver had the band over there. And you know, his person there was Joe Dutre and Baby Dots and Johnny Dots. And he had Lil on the piano. And Bill on the same, Bill Johnson played bass with him. So that was the person that loved that band during that time.
What about have the Lottie Taylor? Oh, Lottie Taylor?
Well, I guess she passed. It's like the rest of a lot of people. She never been married.
She's not around now.

Well, I never did know whether she could have been married then as far as I knew. Yeah. But Joe had several women pianists. It seemed like there was more women pianists who played that type of music than the men. Now there was a pianist up there from here called Arthur Campbell too. He played with George Field in the spot. And later on, fellas like Tom Aladdin came up and Mutt was up there for a while. And they came up, I think Mary Mack, like Mary Mack had, they played at the Monogram Theater. And so they began to, I missed the music, you know, at the beginning until I found out where this different band was. And so I said, well, this is just like New Orleans. I mean, we used to just ramble all night there. We'd go to like a place called the Funky London. And a few of those from then, it's like Bourbon Street. A few of those from there was the dream. And just died and right across the street on the corner, Deluxe. And then you'd keep on State Street and you didn't. He liked number one, he liked number two. And by the time you hit 31st Street then you'd, the place is called Schiller's, this band, this jazz band from Memphis. I think the Memphis Fire plays was playing there then. And so then you'd go on the road, Royal Gardens, Joe was the band. And so that was it. I mean, later on they, later on Joe, when he left there, they changed the name of the place to the Lincoln Gardens. And I was supposed to go to WIC, take the George Fields place. But the place caught on fire Christmas Eve. They changed it from the Royal Gardens to the Lincoln Gardens. And so that made Joe out of jobs. And so Joe went to work with Dave Payton, who later on I worked in this band too. But Joe was only there a short time. Joe was a pretty good businessman. I can't understand why he went down so rapid. But I understand too that it was pyreia, you know. And he never was the same. And he never did come back to me. He was close in the order of him to come back, you know. Like Shreveport and places like that he was band. When I was with Louis Armstrong, we met him in Galveston. But he never did come back. And Freda didn't either. He never did come back to me. So it wasn't long before Joe had his own band at the plantation. Now the plantation would be like he hadn't died or the Red Cross, it was the sunset. And Red Cross Street was the nest. And Jimmy Noon, he would play the 12 o'clock with Dr. Cook's 26 piece band. And then he would have his own band, Earl Hines and Bud Scott and Lawson Buford. I forgot, Johnny Wells drums, yeah. And so in time, Louis went to work. I saw Louis the first when he arrived. I was sitting on the stand. I knew he was coming because I heard Joe, I always say that Brother Dick would be here soon. So true enough, the night he was supposed to come, he did come. And I was sitting on the stand. I'll never forget he had on a sail over the Brownsuit, tan shoes, you know. And he came and he started the very next night. Well, it wasn't long before he set that time on fire. And he stayed there for about two years. So finally he had an offer to join Fletcher Henderson. So he went to New York, he stayed there a year with Fletcher Henderson. He was coming back and joined his wife, Lil. By that time she had the band at the Dreamland. So he went from the Dreamland with Tate at the Vendome. Tate had an orchestra that, at Shellow and instruments like that, about three fields. They played a lot of overtures but they featured Armstrong, you know, and the hot stuff. And he doubled from there to the Sunset with Carol Dickinson's band. So Joe Glazer had the, that was his mother's place, he was running the place. And I'd say the manager, or the boss if you want to call it. And so he and Carol had some woods. So he fired Carol and I saw Lewis come to have the band. So they're shooting at one another all night long. He and Joe, obviously. Yeah, and it was something to see. The place, even back to the Royal Garden about the first ten rows, musician Husker would have. And Paul Morales was there, you know, his band, New Orleans, Little King. And all that, I would say around one o'clock. There was four or five bands there. There was Miff Moe that came down to Venuti and all those bands. They'd come away, we'd have a little vacation, come from far away to New York. And that's where I first saw the Dorset Brothers and one of my favorite trombones, Jack Teagarden. And this boy wrote the similar blues, the Bix. Yeah, they all were there, see, all were there. And Joe Oliver. And then when they moved a few blocks farther south, well, they continued to come around Bing Crawl and all that bunch. You could see them every night. And all up and down 35th night, George Field had a band. And then Tommy Ladner had a band on 35th Street. 35th was just loaded just like Bourbon Street. And they had the entertainers, John Wycliffe had the band of entertainers. And so it just was, some guys had two jobs. Everybody that wanted to work could play great. And some of them had two jobs.
Did you ever see Big Jim Coliseum around?
I saw him. Yeah, I saw him in his place, but I don't remember seeing him in one of those places.
He didn't come around to him. He might have.

You didn't see him? No, I didn't know him until later on, you know. Yeah, it was maybe a year or so before he was killed, assassinated. But he could have, and I worked for it. I worked for Capone's brother, Ralph. Yeah, the syndicate had the grand tier, so the Hood Heinz bands. A fellow by the name of Fox, Ed Fox, was the front and the manager I'd say. And so I worked for him. And then his brother had a place called Cotton Club. The late Walter Barnes played there sometimes too. He's a fellow that brought up in Natchez.
Yeah, where was he from, anyhow, really?
Well, when I first knew Walter, he was in Chicago.
Yeah.

So I couldn't say just where he was from. But I played with him, two engagements before he'd taken that ill-fated tour. And the Providence Hospital had some kind of benefit. And it was another club, it was a large club. And so he hired me for the two engagements. Well, he didn't ask me to make the trip, and I didn't want to go. I didn't ask him to go either, because I just figured he wasn't going to pay me the money I'd like to have. So when he was burned up in the fire and some of his men, naturally, when I was taking the picture of the band doing these two engagements, there I was in the picture. So I was denying I was dead for about a couple of months. I thought you had burned him. No, I'm still alive and breathing, you know, one of those things. Yeah.
What about Johnny Torrio? Did you ever see him? Johnny Torrio?
If I did, I didn't know him. Yeah. You see what I'm talking about? Because in these places, it was known gangsters that frequented the places. They were there?
They were in there every night, yeah.

And I'll tell you one thing that really frightened me, and also the band. You see, in 31 we came down here and opened up at the Suburban Gardens. Well, we were broadcast from a place called the Showboat in Chicago, and they heard us, you know. So they engaged Louie to come down here and play. That's the time so many bands met us at the train, you know, at the big parade on Canal Street. Well, we were playing there, and a little bit of my story, Louie, about his time, began his popularity, began to climb, I'd say. I'd use that expression. And I was playing Savoy with H. and Tate, Chiquari in Chicago. And he came through, so in the mission he came over and talked to me, he said, well, he called me Nosy. He said, well, Nosy, I'm going to California, LA, and I'm going to the Sebastian's Cotton Club. And he used Les Heights band out there. He said, but I'll be back in about three months and I want you to play trombone for me. Well, I forgot all about it, so he did, truly his word. They're looking for me around, I live right around the corner from him, looking for me a couple of weeks, you know. And so finally, the guys around there knew he was looking for me. And so finally, they made contact and we start the rehearsals. So we go down the showboat and got a couple of weeks. And his former manager, Rockwell, he and Rockwell had some trouble. Anyhow, his manager later on was Dan Collins, who was a lawyer. So we were playing one night and it came a long distance call from New York. He went in the phone booth and there was a fellow who called a gangster called Foster. He went in there with him and put his gun on and said, come on, you're going back in New York. And Louis said, no, I'm not going back in New York. And he didn't. So thereafter, every night, he had to be a scooter by a squad call, you know. So we stayed there three months. And then we started doing this one night, through Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky. And so finally the word came, I said, where we going in New York? Well, I was glad to be in my hometown, you know. And that's when we came down and worked out there three months at Suburban Garden.
You know, we're forgetting about where you went to school and all that. Oh, no, I'm not forgetting.

I attended, you see, I, we rented from some people by the name of Lavazzo. So some of our neighbors was, uh, the Champ and B-Sent, the Lavazzo and the Palmers. I remember that very well. And, uh, when I first entered the school, elementary school, I entered in fifth grade, because they had, uh, there's a school teacher. She was a graduate from Straits University. Uh, our landlord's daughter, Camille, her name was. So I went to this pay school. And so when I, when I, when I first attended Tomlin' Farm, I started in, uh, fifth grade, but they did put me back to fourth grade, see. Uh-huh. And so I, I graduated from there. And then, uh, the next was, uh, uh, McDonald's school. It was up in Carleton there. And then from there, I graduated from there and I went to New Orleans University. I went there one year, about one semester. That was up on, uh, uh, Valley Martins in St. Charles. I understand now those schools are all in Moores and Dillard. Yeah. Yeah. At that time they had Lillard University, Southern University, St. University, New Orleans University, and later on it's Catholic, uh, Institutionally School.
What's they just doing?
Yeah, the old magazine was out there, yeah. I remember when it was built, when they was building it.
What was Camille's last name?
Camille Lab is over. That is V-I-Z-Z-O-R, I think that you, you spelled it that way.
Who was the music teacher at New Orleans University?

Well, uh, I'll tell you, I remember the president's name, his name, he was from Boston, his name was Dr. Darling. But the only music I had there was, uh, was vocal, you know, though it ran me fast over one of those things, you know. So I don't quite remember. I remember one of the teachers I had, Mrs. Ennis, uh, I can't forget her because every day we went to chapel. Mm-hmm. And she would go about 11.30, staying until 12. And she'd keep her eye on me, and I'd be next, right, kept me right next to her all the time, you know, sitting right next to her. So I couldn't hardly forget that. We'd sing, you know, and at 12 o'clock, it was out. Now during that time, Udy Sankton was attending that too. But I didn't know him, you know, I didn't know him as well as I did later on.
You weren't a bad boy or anything? Oh no, no.

I'd never been to drugs, that's good. I'd never been to trouble. The only time I would have been in trouble, if you may recall, they put us all in jail in Memphis, the whole band. See we played, we did six weeks and when we left, see it was supposed to be a big dance here at the end of this game out there. And it's supposed to have some government warehouse or something like that. Anyhow, people came far away from Florida and Mississippi, you know, and Ramport Street and the people just, these little flippers, you know, all of them down Ramport Street. And you could see it was from out of town. Anyhow, it's a dance that was booked and never came off. They wouldn't let the people in the place. And so we left that night and opened up at Houston, Texas. We had 12,000 people there the first night and the second night, the second night was about somewhere around 4 or 5,000. So we played six weeks and then we went to Fort Worth, Dallas, Waco, and Galveston. Then we crossed over to Oklahoma and played Oklahoma City and Tulsa first. And then we doubled right back into Texas again and played the same place over. That's when we ran into Joe Oliver's band. He had a good band. Most musicians are in New York, see. By that time Joe was in New York. And that's the last, oh yeah, I did see him once in Chicago after that. So we, then we went on and we played Shreeport, it's a football game. I think Xavier was playing somebody. It's only in college, he's in Texas. And then we went on to Jackson, Mississippi. We played Jackson, Mississippi. And then after that's when the trouble began. We was on our way to Memphis, to Leroy. And there was two bus drivers, so John Collins was in New York. He was booking this RKO circuit. So the band was different charges. His wife, her name was Mary Collins. And so her and Louis were sitting together, talking business. And they kept switching on the light, on and off, at short intervals I'd say. About, they'd do it about twice a minute. Yeah, and so we didn't pay much attention to it. We didn't know that trouble was brewing. So when we reached Memphis, the superintendent there said, well, come on you guys, get out of there. So she told her, I said, no. I said, I paid, it was different than the money I paid. Because we were making this long jump from Jackson to Little Rock. And he said, boy, it's tiresome as a little cheap bus, a smaller bus, you know. So they had this hassle, they went on for about five minutes. So he told the driver, he said, well, drive on over to the terminal. So when we arrived at the terminal, it looked like half of the Memphis police force was there. So they put us all in jail, but the Vandale player, Mike McKenzie, I don't know how he escaped, because he was riding the bus with us. So they put us all in jail. So they mugged us and kept us in there about maybe an hour and we were supposed to double back and play the palace on Beale Street in Memphis. And so he bailed us out. And we had two women along with us and a guy around me called Professor Cook and Joe Lindsey. Joe was supposed to give Louis for his job. He was a drummer. And so we arrived in Little Rock about eleven o'clock that night and we played about two. And we doubled back to Memphis. The train was held up for us and we doubled back and we broadcast at the Peabody Hotel in Memphis. And here's where we were frightened again. We were playing and finally Louis said, ladies and gentlemen, I'm now going to dedicate a number to the Memphis Police Department. I'd be glad when you did. You rascal you. And so I recognized some of the policemen, you know. But they were smiling but I kind of figured it was a trickeration. I couldn't play hard. My lips was, my teeth was chattering, you know. And so after they moved the screen, they moved the screen and they made a wild dash towards us. And we couldn't run any farther and we backed up and we were, we're not going to hurt you boys. We're not going to hurt you boys. He says, we understand you're going to play a middle-drammel. So he's at the palace. We will be there. And true enough, I'd say about the first seven or eight rows was the police and the families. That midnight ramble. So we're headed for trouble again. Louis Armstrong had a lot of trouble. I mean a lot of people don't know it. I know a lot of things about Louis, I never tell. Yeah. And the first thing he had was wife trouble. He and Lil was on bad terms and it was this alpha, this, she should have been the, about the third wife. She was along with her, you know. And most everywhere we'd go, Lil would be coming right along a little later. And so we left there and went to St. Lucid in St. Louis. I remember that very well because that was a great series between the Yanks and the Cardinals, which the Cardinals won. And for the first three shows the booters and there was a whole lot of noise. And so one of the big shots came down from New York and finally things were smoothed out. And then we're on the R.R. Hill now. Then we head off there, we played the chauffeur's club. That's a great place through those days. Charlie Creff, you might have heard of him, and Dewey Jackson, you know. They were featured there. And then we left there and went to the Albion Cincinnati. Then we doubled back from Cincinnati to the Palace in Chicago, then the Palace in Cleveland. And then we started playing this one-nighters through West Virginia. I understood Earl Humphreys in West Virginia during that time, but I didn't see him. We was in Huntington, you know. We played Huntington and we played Louis Abel during Derby time. In Ohio, one-nighters in some parts of Michigan. Then we jumped from there to the Pearl Theater in Philadelphia, where they had that blue law there, you know. We couldn't start until about a minute after twelve. So they had what they called a, well it was a regular circuit. And there was some brothers by the name of the Stiefel Brothers. In New York at that time they had this old Lafayette Theater. So we played the Pearl and then we went to New York and played the Lafayette. And then we went and called it Around the World. Then we went to Washington and then Baltimore. And then back to Philly again to stand the theater. And then we came back to New York and we played in Jersey City. And then we went to Connecticut. And here comes the house again. And the old movie star, Ruth Rowland, she was the headliner. You don't understand how the headliners last. So Louis had come on right before and he stopped the show every time. See? And so she began to get angry. So then she asked for the arena so that she'd come on ahead of Louis. Well, he stopped the show as a headliner too. And so, we was just there a week and then we went up to Boston. And that's where we had the great battle with the Castle Loma and Fletcher Henderson and Louis Armstrong Band. That was right out of Boston. And that was some battle. And these Castle Lomas had the term to use during that time was cutting, you know, and whoever best the other band. And they met this great band they called the Cotton Pickers, McKinney's Cotton Pickers out of Detroit, see. They played opposite Dean Goldkett there in Detroit. And these fellas all bandaged up. The piano player had his head all bandaged up. Two or three of them was all bandaged up. But those guys really played. People still talk about it in New England. About that battle of jazz. So then we came back to our store along the island. We made a couple of shots. Well, I'll make a mouth in the shot. I'll be glad you did. You were asking them to assume he was using it, you know. And we did a lot of recording. In fact, every chance we got, Louis the record was selling like hotcakes then on an OK record, you know. So finally we were supposed to come back to New Orleans. He wanted us back to New Orleans. We had three places that wanted the band. And one of them was in France and one was here and that was in California. So he disbanded the band, Collins did. And Louis went back to Sebastian's. And so I never did play with Louis anymore. We still were friends, you know, whenever we were in Chicago. I'd always, Louis, see, by that time he had the wife that he had when he died, you know. He and Alf were married and they separated, see. But I do believe that Lil had never stopped loving Louis. I'll tell you why. You know one of the funny questions. We were in Massachusetts. I was with the Franz Jackson band. She was playing piano with us. It's been about four years ago. So we began to talk. And if you just judge the way she talked you figured she hated him, you know. So her and I engaged in an argument. I said Louis still was the best in the world. And so she said that Jonah Jones could outplay him. Well in spite of talking like that, I found out later that she just was talking, that's all. So here she still loved him. Because I found out they still exchanged in spite of being Lucille, that was his last wife, you know. When he died that was his wife. And so they exchanged presents. And when he died she flew up there as quick as she could get. And it wasn't long after he died that she died. She fell dead. They ran on the TV, had him, you know. It was one of these things. It was, yeah. It's pertaining to Louis Armstrong. I forget.
Memorial. Yeah, something like that.

Yeah. And she fell off the pen and dead and heart attack. So I attribute that to her grieving. She never forget him. And I did have a little hassle on her. This tune strutting with some barbecue. I understand she said it was his and she said it was hers. Well you know Lil was a very good musician. You see she graduated from some college down in Tennessee. They'd get together and one would make a few notes, another would make a few notes and look around and they had a tune. All those tunes like dip them out and things like that, Canal Street Blues, they were right on the stand doing working hours you know. And so this Harmon's dreaming. The elevator ran right, the tracks was right over the top of it. And they needed a big band like that in order for the people to hear the band. And so it's a 26 piece band. But when Freddie started to blow in, they really heard it.
He was stronger than always.

Oh yeah, he's about the strongest of all the fellas. Joe Oliver was strong. But you see Joe Oliver, he did a whole lot of playing mutes. Joe Oliver had large hands. Yeah, yeah, yeah. This eccentric and some other tunes.
And he would get the rooster crow or anything like that?

And then we had a fellow named, see what it was? Jimmy who?
Jimmy Strode.

S-T-O-R-O-D-E. Conant? Yeah, Trum. He was good too. Yeah, a lot of fellows used to have him. You never heard of Nene Bryant even had him. He was a drummer, a good one. And he played piano. So then this fellow came up that was beating out at the Irish Channel, his jaw was broken. Later on I read that he started playing the bass fiddle then. Recall.

Recall, Ellix. And then we got Lee Collins, he came up. And then Snagg Jones came up, he left, he had been playing with Celestan. And then comes Tommy Ladner. Tommy Ladner came up. So the piano player would take and play their parts out, you know, and they'd get their parts and they still built a nice band.

And I had this, when I recorded in 1946, we still, still do. We'll get as many New Orleans musicians as possible. I mean until today. And so Lee used to play with the mouthpiece right across his bottom lip. So I kept laughing and finally I got into the corner of the trumpet like it should be. I regret this because I figured that there was another fellow by the name of Lewis Ogletree, who was right down there, this was at the Union. And I got him and said, I just couldn't, I didn't use Lee. And so he and I, it was a bad feeling from then on, you understand. I wasn't so with Lee, but there's some things that I figured he did. There was a fellow around, a young fellow that came to some nice money, and he was booking these bands concerts, you know. And I had rehearsed the band pretty good, and I never did get a chance to play. And I figured maybe something might happen, I don't know. But he and Lee was like this, you understand. So, but as you grow older you learn, I could have used Lee just to play some hot choruses, you see. Then I never would have lost his friendship. But you learn, you see that afterwards, you know what I'm talking about. And so, as you know, when Lee went over to Ory, he and Zuby Singleton, Melrose, not Melrose, Meshro, they went over to Europe. And Lee, something happened to his chest or throat. He came back sick, and he never did recover. He laid on about three or four years before he died. And so, I think of that sometimes, you know. He was a fellow, you know, old. It could have been another way. It could have been another way. I might have talked to the guy and said, Well, I want to use another trumpet, which would have made it three brass. But then the time, then I had trouble clearing this, Don L. You see, when you have a contract for a certain day, a certain amount of men, well, you don't want to go to the fellow and say, Well, I can't make it today, and after bed, make it next week or something like that. It just, it puts you in a bad light, I imagine, you understand? But I hated that because Lee and I attended school together. We only lived at Louisiana and me and Ferrette and I lived on the other shades between Howard and Ferrette. It's right around the county. So Lee died. And I hated that because now I see it could have been another way. Maybe I could have used him just the same, just in spots. But we did have things arranged. He would have to test it and I don't play. You know, and maybe we'd have a course and I'd give him a course or something like that. It was possible.
I understand they tried to put him in the rest of the spare for a while. Yeah.

No, he could play, he really could play. But he didn't read so well. Now a guy, Kelly, a guy Kelly could read and play good too. Who taught you to read?
Oh well, it's between, well my first teacher, I'd forgotten him, was William Robinson. What's his name?
William Robinson.

He was from God? Yeah, you see, I didn't care for the trombone when I did become interested, because I used to whistle a lot of clarinet parts, I'd say. And right up until there I can do that. So I returned home one evening, I'd say in the afternoon, and I walked inside and I walked into my room and I saw a little green bag. And so I went there, kind of curious, you know. Yeah, yeah, Dutre taught me, Roy taught me more so. And then I, later on as I progressed, I joined Eli Rice's band. I stayed with him about 14 months. We traveled all through Wisconsin and Minnesota and Michigan, Michigan and Minnesota. And I used to get out there in them woods and practice. So after 14 months I came back to Chicago and I played the great pianist Teddy Weller for him at the Dream. And Shirley Clare was on the cornet myself and Teddy and I had forgotten the fellow who could play drum and sing very well. And I think Artis Starks was on there, Clownet and Sax. So we came back pain night and Padlock was on the police. I know 5250 was paying us. I knew we'd get that money. I just said married too. And so I, then I went and joined Arthur Sims in Milwaukee, Wisconsin Roof. And so after about a year, with Arthur, Arthur caught me in August and died. So then, the fellow who was now, is a physician. He, Arthur Albright, he was the oldest man in the band. He was a guitar player in the band, the band, the band of yours. And he taken over the band and he left to go to Mayharry to study medicine. That's what Oscar Bernie Young. Now he and I were schoolmates too, at the time we were from school. So, I had played with him in discipline called the Paramount. . . . .
I think Audis Starks was on there, Clamondon and Saxe.

So we came back, Pay Night and Padlock was on the place. I know 5250 was paying us. I didn't really get that money, I just said married to. And so then I went and joined Arthur Sims in Milwaukee at the Wisconsin Roof. And so after about a year with Arthur, Arthur caught pneumonia in August and died. So then a fellow who is now a physician, Arthur Albright, he was the oldest man in the band. He was a guitar player and banjoist. So he was taking over the band and then he left to go to Meharry to study medicine. That's when Oscar Burney Young, now he and I were schoolmates too, we had a time to come to school. So I had played with him in this record for Paramount, previous to that, before he ever joined Sims up in Wisconsin. And that's some of the stuff that's on this record now. But between the two leaders, Arthur Albright and Bernie Sims. And in this particular band we had Edward Inge, did you ever hear, he used to play with Don Redmond. He made that famous tune, Channel the Weed. And we had Cas No Simpsons, he was a great pianist. And we had Gilbert Mundy, Burt Bailey, those were saxophonists, Gilbert, Double on the Fiddler. So I began to take some lessons in Milwaukee, the president of this white union there, see. I'd taken lessons in him about five, six months. And then we left there and we went to Savoy. And in fact we went to Indianapolis, the brother Tom's place up there, the Indiana roof, Indianapolis. This was the Wisconsin roof. So after two weeks when we came back we didn't have no job, probably by the name of Grant Moore. His band was in there and Grant Moore had a chicken train, he used to run across the stage, you know. A what?
A chicken.
A trained chicken?
Yeah.

He'd play music, he'd trance all across the street. It was a novelty, you know. A dancing chicken? Well he'd strut kind of like he was dancing, you know. You could call it a dancing rock. So after that we stayed around Chicago, I mean Milwaukee, and gave our own dances. We would just draw away from the Wisconsin roof, where we was popular, we had been there six years. There was two bands there, Bill Costner's band. Well we wasn't allowed to play any waltzes. We could. But this other band was more on the street or the street, you know. They didn't play jazz as well as we did. Because then we got Zill and Randolph taking a mouse-randolph place, later on the mouse played with Cal Calaway. And Zill was the guy that was the music director for Louis Armstrong. He wrote this old man Moses day, you know. And so then we opened up in the Savoy in Chicago, three nights a week. And we left there and we went down to Tulsa. Then we jumped from Tulsa to, we thought it was going to be a little interesting place to call Miami, Oklahoma. We were on our way to a long jump from Tulsa to Lansing, Michigan. So we, just outside of Miami, a woman kept, she had one of these T models. We had three cars. We had a Whippet, Willis Knight, and a Buick. And she just, it was cutting right sharp across us, you know. And so our bad luck to leave this battery, we had a Willis Knight that split wide open. So when we made it into Miami, a crowd gathered there, you know. And so they began to keep calling going. Well, there's a fellow right across the street. He had a large garage and he said, you fellas come on in. He said, look like you may get in some trouble. So he drove all the way to Joplin, Missouri and obtained a battery and came back and said, you know. And so they told us, don't let dark kick you. But when darkness came, we ate them clay, the red clay. We was in Joplin. So, and then we couldn't get in to eat, sing to eat. Then we went on to St. Louis and we ate. And then we finally made it up to Lansing. So I stayed with him about two or three weeks. And then Dave Payton had the band at the Regan.
What was the name of that band then?
Yeah, that was the Boynton Young's band. Oh, yeah.
That's the name of the band?

Yeah. And about this time he had Raymond Valentine on trumpet. And he had Eddie Belfield. You might have heard of him, Eddie Belfield. And Willow Morin, we had a, and a fellow by. Doc? Hmm? Doc Morin?
Yeah.

Doc Willow? Yeah. Yeah. And Raymond Valentine. And we had Cass Simpson on piano and accordion. And we had Boris Lovingood. He's from, I think Austin, Texas. And we had the, we had the, five brass. So they were working out of this Greystone ballroom in Detroit. So they were booked there. We played the Matinee on Sunday and played that evening too. So we knew this coming, we'd been to Detroit and heard the band. We knew they had a good band. So we had three arrangers in the band so we had a whole lot of singing you know. And we played a whole lot of this, all of the college tunes you see. We played like Indiana, you know, really jazz, you see. So that's how we came down to Chicago to play for fraternity you know. And they heard that we played these college tunes. That's how I came to get the job at Savoy. But so we decided, we said well, we'll just play some stocks and just appear mediocre you know. So we came in around, I think it was something around five o'clock, something like that. And they stood around and heard it. So I imagine they said well, hear nothing to this you know. But later on at night when they started playing by the eight o'clock, we showered down to them. So they, down, down taking the band in the back of the dressing room and rehearsed them. Yeah, it was on Easter Sunday, I never forget that. Yeah, he taking that band in the back and we were together, see we've been together about six years. Maybe a man or so you know, in exchange you know. So then it goes after leaves, after leaves, and we went up to Lansing. So I quit him, I was making $110 in 1929, no tax coming out of the regal, you know. And you see my best experience I'd say would be, was the brass band. This 165th band was a wartime band, you know in the Army. And the fellow by the name of Art Stewart, that was a conductor, he was a fellow that had a high soprano voice like, alright, get in there, you know. He frightened the heck out of me to begin with. But then I found out that it wasn't, he didn't mean it, he didn't mean it. So I'd go and rehearse with him every Sunday. And overtures such as morning, noon and night, 1812 and things like. And hot strasses, marches, a whole lot of them tough marches, you know. And so that's when I, my first time in New York was 1924. I went there with the, it was a Nathapithias Convention. And then fanfare and everything, such things as that. And then we'd go right up under, right through this dressing room right back, see, and then go up on the stage and do stage presentation. So I guess Louis was hearing about me all the time because when he hit Chicago, he chews me, which would cause a lot of jealousy, you know. Well, that's when he's homeboy, you see. Joe.

Yeah, Joe. And then we had this guy, Charles Levere. And we had Zooty, and then we had Bill and Huey Long, Huey Long guitar player, Bill was a bass player. He committed suicide, so to say, about a year or so ago. Some people say he didn't, some say he's a nice bass player. Anyhow, we did the recording. And I heard him recently, and it did sound bad. But I understand she's living in New York State now. But we never did receive any money from that. Never did.
That would have been a good time to get some money. Yeah. 1935. Yeah.
So you played mostly with the reading bands, that were you?
Oh yeah, yeah. Up until recently. I had to. Well, no, I'm glad you asked this question. Now I'm supposed to play tonight. Now I've heard Louie Nelson.
Yeah.

Now I want you to understand me. I never knock another musician. I mean it doesn't do you any good. It hurts you, not the musician. Then you make an enemy for life. Now I've heard Louie Nelson, I've heard this other Jim Robinson, and I've heard some trombone players here. Now where Danny Barker was playing, there's a trombone player there. He sounded pretty good in his German fellow. He sounded nice. And I'm not fine with Jim Robinson, nobody. They're friends of mine. All I'm saying is that I had to get away from the style of Nelson and Jim Robinson, because the fellows began to tell me as the music progressed, say in the 50s, going to sections and everything, and the solo, well they didn't want me to play bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop. But I can. I'll say, not brag, I'm flexible. See I can play most of any category, because I've had training, Marquette Extension University, for a theory and harmony and stuff like that, you understand? I've been in the theater, I've been in the brass band, and I've been in the bands when they had sections when I had to take and blend with the two other trombones. So I've taken a little bit from here, a little bit from there, a little bit from there. See? I'm not saying the way I play is just strictly my style. I'm saying that I gather something from Rob Palmer, I've got something from Dutre, and even a little touch of Tea Gardens, and other Fred Robinson. You know, people sound good to me when I go home and practice. It's a mixture, you see what I'm talking about? And so, I can play Dixieland, you understand? As you'll hear me, I can play Dixieland, but when it comes to my solo, then I'm a little more modern than Roberson and the other fellas, you understand what I'm talking about? I'm more on the order, the German boy and the other fellas, you understand? Not too high. My range is Bb and sometimes C, but not way up there. I can play there as far as F, but I don't find it necessary. You see, I don't find it necessary. I can get plenty out of, from Bb, which is just occasionally Ab. And that G and that Eb and that, I can get plenty out of, right down there. It's plenty. And you have some body. You see? But the high notes are not necessary.
No. But it's low instrument, right?
Well it's flatty.
Now there's Vic Dickerson.

Now I like the way Vic Dickerson plays. See now he plays up there you know. He's smooth. He has a nice intonation. You see what I'm talking about? I love the way Jack Teagarden sang and played, you understand? I met Jack in Texas years ago. I always liked the way he played. I liked the way he sang just like he played. So I've taken a little bit from a lot of fellas. I'm not all that original. But my background and the foundation is New Orleans. I can make those glisters as you'll hear me. You know when I was singing. So what did he say? So I can play that. Because I started playing that way. And as you find on these records, you see, you'll find that I play a lot of different sounds than I did on this record.
Yeah. But even then your vibrato sounds a little different to me.
Yeah, yeah.
I noticed something different in the Tin Roof Blues.
Yeah.
It didn't sound like, say, Bernie's is vibrato at all.
No, no.
Now how did you produce your vibrato back in the early days?

Well, to be truthful about the vibrato, I didn't pay any attention to the vibrato. You see, we'll just take Dutre for instance. Dutre and Zoo Robin was smooth. There was no one who played them shelly parts. And as you've heard Dutre when he played the jazz solos, his was a bit different than Roy. Roy would take a pair or something, you know, and put it over the bellies and it was rough, you know, gut bucket I'd say. Yeah. Now Roy, I'd come to Ory again. Ory was rough too. Yeah. But between the two, Ory couldn't touch Roy. But Ory composed two, muscat rambling things like Ory's Creole trombone. He was Louis Hot Five, and things like that. And so, and out in California, I was on the air, you know, in that picture. And so Ory just, the people just put him in a different category than Roy.
He's a much slicker character. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

He's a pretty good businessman. Yeah, yeah, but Roy was the best trombone player ever left here. Now there's one fellow way years ago I heard, see I used to sit on the stand with Joe, Oliver and his band, and him talking about these different bands, and there was one trombonist that his name was Baptiste Delaney, and he said he was the best he ever heard. But this is what's supposed to happen to Baptiste. He lost his mind, and he used to climb the lamppost, you know, with his trombone. And of course a lot of people don't believe in this, but they claim that this house where he lived, when he decided to tear this house down, or wreck it, they said he found between that mortar and stuff, his long underwear, stretch, an arm there, an arm there, and the legs, here and like that. And as soon as he tore that house down he regained his senses. But they say he was the best that they ever heard. That included all of them. But Roy was a good musician. Roy could read, Roy could play more than one instrument, you know. And he'd better read, a better musician than ever.
Did you ever hear Earl Humphrey play?
No, I never did. And I'm sad about that because you see the thing-
Even as a kid you never heard of?

No. Earl was playing way before me, you know. He played with Emmanuel Perez around 1915. See I didn't leave here until 1917 with my parents. But I still had, I used to pass by the Humphreys, you know, and here they played. I saw the grandfather and the father.
They still had Cadiz and Liberty.

Yeah, same place. And right around on Jenna I think it was, the two hall boys, they're the cousins to the Humphreys, you know. And I used to see them carrying the instruments. But still, I never thought about playing in the music, you see. And so you take, for instance, the vibrato you spoke about. I used to get more or less a straight tone, you understand. And when I first noticed that my tone was changing, I get more of a vibrato now than ever. I got that, I started that because different trombone players, I liked the tone like Lawrence Brown, I even liked Seagarden, Higginbotham. See, all those fellas, they've always been ranked over me, even Ory. But Ory, not bragging, Ory has never been a trombone player. I am. I'm raised a pretty good musician, you know, all around musician. And I think now I play more of a trombone than he ever played. That's just my opinion. And so I'm with Louie at the Palace in Cleveland. So I'm practicing the dressing room. First was, then we went to Chicago theater, and Chicago was a fellow there in the pit band. I was noodling around in my hand playing a little jazz. And so he came and introduced himself. He wanted to take some lessons for me. So I said, well, the guy like this, I hear him with them big round tones in on him, his bottom notes, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, triple tongue and all that stuff. I said, well, the guy like this, he wanted to take lessons from me. Well, there's a lot of jealousies, I foresaid, at the union there. Now, Willie Hightower's wife was the financial secretary, see, and she'd throw a few crumbs my way, but otherwise if you didn't go up there and blast those dice and gamble. The guys used to come up there in their tuxedos ready to go to work. They'd go to work and Boyd Hall would go around and pick them up after they finished and bring them up there to gamble and play poker. Well if you didn't go up there and gamble, people would call you up. And unless Miss Hightower got over to it, well, just like this fellow came, you know, came out of the union to see me about taking some lessons. But they told them about another guy and I didn't see him anymore. So I'm in Cleveland and finally I found out I'm doing something wrong. My tunes became broader and I'm getting a little more vibrato. You see what I'm talking about? So now, the way I play now, I use more vibrato than that. Anytime a trumpet player with me, like in the band I've been playing in Chicago, well the leader asked him to use a little more vibrato in order for the match with me. You see, I like it on playing particularly some sweet tune, and I do love to play like tune like getting sentimental over you and things like that you know. And I'm striving right as of yet. I'm still trying, I'm striving for intonation. I mean I'm 71 years old but I still figure I can improve. I am improving. See what I'm talking about? I am improving. And I figure there isn't as much as I intend to play music most likely until I die. Well why not try to get better?
Well do you use lip or diaphragm or something?

Well I can get it from the lip but I use the hand, but not too much hand. I got a way of getting the vibrato by just shaking my horn, you know, and getting in a certain position. It's just about shaking it like this I get it, instead of all the way, like this. You can move the whole horn.
Yeah.
I got this from Dutre and Roy, you know, like this, the vibrato.
Then we use slide.
Yeah. But now, but now I use a little lip and I just can shake it like this and I can enrich my tone. Just shake it like that.
Well sometimes it sounds like you're using lip trills like T-Garden would.
Well I do, I use a lot of, I'd say about sixty, seventy percent of my working jazz is lip trills. Yeah, lip trills. I use a lot of lip trills.
Do you go down into, well you know Roy always said he could play his horn backwards. Yeah. In the six and seven position, do you use that? Or do you go down first and second?

Well I tell you, Claude Jones I think was one of the great trombones, used to be the Fletcher Anderson. Claude, I noticed this playing Dickie Wells and all them fellas. See I always go, whenever this fella was in town, I'd go there, as I said before. And I tried to, I copied, I'm a copycat, see what I'm talking about? And I'd go back home and work on it. Now some leaders don't like much vibrato. You suppose if you're in a section, I mean you suppose a match of tones, you understand what I'm talking about? So Roy, oh yeah when it comes to these, like that low E natural down in the seventh position, well that don't require too much vibrato. The pretty notes are, the notes are in the staff and as high as like G, F and like that, you know, and the B flat and C and things like that. But down there, they always want me to just give them a big tone down there, you know, and a lift and that E natural down there, you see. And so, and that's what I've been trying to do. See I practice every day here in Chicago, an hour and a half, two hours a day. I'm striving now more harder than I did earlier, see what I'm talking about? Because I'm beginning to become a little more recognized now. You see I'm getting in demand, I'd say, that's why I'm down here I figure, because somebody spoke for me, you understand? And if I wasn't producing, they wouldn't speak for you, you understand what I'm talking about? But you'll find out that it's going to be a little different when I play tonight. It's going to be, some of this fellow here, I'm not so great that I didn't hear him and couldn't like him, or the German, I like both of them. It's only the 40, well I imagine it's kind of by the way it's like, you understand what I'm talking about? But they both have nice big tones, you know? And so that's what I love, is a nice tone.
When you first started playing, were you playing with Bantam, you were all playing your arrangements? The first band that you played with, was Bernie and John?
With Bernie, what you asked me about, Bernie?
When you made those recordings like in 1923, 24, were you using arrangements with those bands? No, no arrangements.

Then you were at living on the one? Yeah, at living, that's right. And I've always felt more freely at living than when I'm reading the music. You see now this recording we made just a few days ago, we had this skeleton arrangements, you know, behind Edith Wilson, the old singer Edith Wilson. Well we had, she had a background, we just caused, you know? And then spots where certain guys take solos. Now I recorded two of my own tunes. I sang on this, which I'm not much of a singer, but I think it may pass on Goodbye Mr. Blues. And I had another tune, I called it Dilsa's Blues. And so we recorded both of those. Do you have the music to those numbers?
Huh? Do you have a lead sheet to those numbers?
I have a lead sheet to them, yeah. I just sent a, I can.
You might want to tell the player. Huh?

Well I can, I might can obtain it from you, for you rather, from Leon Scotty. Leon Scotty, we called him Scotty, his name is Scott Leon Scotty, the trumpet player, because he made me a lead sheet. And I had, I gave Brother Montgomery the money, to send the money in to have it copyrighted, you know? And so I'll write to him right away. I'll write tonight or this afternoon and tell him to make me up a lead sheet. Now he may charge two or three dollars for that, you understand? But he will do it for me. He's a nice trumpet player too. So that's my story. I mean I'm still, yeah I start out that way. But I could read. But I could read music.
Then you became, even when you played with all those bigger band reading matches, you still play ad-libs?

Yeah well I'm not bragging but this is the category I was in. Whenever a band came to Rega Theater short of a trombone player, they used to look at me. There was Bo Moose Johnson or something like that. Jackson. Jackson. And there was Ella Fitzgerald. I played about five or six different bands, you know, short of trombone player. And they sent for me. And there wasn't a rehearsal, you understand? Jimmy Newman sent for me. They put the music on. I was able to play it, you understand what I'm talking about? Okay. Boy, it's living good, taking care of today.

Well anyway, when we started talking about the first band you played with, you know, with Bernie Young and this guy. Buddy Young. Yeah and you played, you said it was mostly Ad-lib. Yeah Ad-lib. Now I want to ask you from the beginning one of the questions I want to ask. How old were you when you came to Chicago?
When I arrived in Chicago, I was 15, I was going on 16 years old.
And you hadn't started playing all that?
No, no I wasn't thinking about playing. And what gave you the idea of playing? My mother wanted me to play. Well she wanted you to play. Yeah, yeah.
And how old were you when you started?
When I started, I must have been about, maybe 18 years old. Yeah. Because I joined the union in 21.
So you started way later than like the early movement.
Oh yeah. I was behind Lee Carlton, I was behind Joe Rochelle, behind the Humphries.
Then you had good teachers. Yeah, I had good teachers.

You were lucky to have very good teachers. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well the technology to me, I just stayed right in front of them all the time. I worried them, you know. Yeah. See Roy and his wife room with us. And I'd live for him in the kitchen. Well you had a good opportunity.
Yeah, I'd live for him.
I'm going to go when I leave and practice a little bit, make my lift too flexible, you know. Because I'd like to do good tonight, you know. Yeah.
But anyway, so you started taking lessons when you were about 18 years old. And then when did you start playing music?

Well then, I'll tell you what happened. I've forgotten about this. I returned in the Orleans in 1921. That's when I met Chester's artists. They were advertising. And I rode on the truck. While I'm still in the preliminary stages. So. You hadn't played any jobs yet. Well I played some with a little band, with Bernie Young, Al Simeon, Omar Simeon, Jimmy McHenry, and people like that, you know. And we were non-union. Just 15? Yeah, we were non-union then. Well we could read a little. You see, yeah, we was reading a little bit. Because we had to be, when we all went in there, this business there, a big tall fella about down there eight feet named Monroe. He chased his catches on them jobs, you know, and run us off the job. So it finally ran us into the union. So we had to take examination. Oh yeah. And Clarence Jones, great pianist, had the band at the Howard's Theater. He was one of the guys that examined us. They put the music right up there and we had to play it. And we played it. So I came back to New Orleans and I was with Renny every day. Get Renny every day. He was playing up in San Susie. And we placed some girls right up there, me and Clarence, right in the neighborhood where I was raised. We'd go to their house every day and Renny and them liked wine and stuff. And I never cared much for the strong stuff, you know. I'm a sweet guy. I like a chemical or something sweet, you know. If it was wine, it was a sweet wine I'd like. But so I hung around Renny and I sent him with Maurice French. Now I love this play. It was a trombone play, wasn't it? No, a trombone play. It was a good one too. He played that, Renny played, My Muscle's Loom It On. And Maurice would sing against the middle of the sea. You know, a regular obligato right with it. Maurice is a nice trombone play. And they had Zepp Renneas I think is his name. And one of the Mareros, he's a Simon, he's a brother. And Joe Renne and Renne himself, no piano. So they played about two or three nights a week up there to San Susie. And I was around about a month or so, I had Bernie Young send some music. But some of the guys in the band didn't read, you know. But I used to like to hear them play Climax, Rag. And Renne and them used to play the blues in C sharp. Now that's the thing about a lot of them guitar players around here, them blues singers. They can't play with us and we can't play with them because they don't have no particular key. Wherever they pick out a melody, a lot of them D flat or G flat or C sharp or F sharp or E natural, anything you know. And let's face it, the average musician has his pet tunes and his pet keys. There's some keys that we all can play better than others. And a B flat instrument, sharp usually bother them if they're not playing them right regularly, you know. And so that's why I never could play with Muddy Waters or some of those blues artists around Chicago because you don't know what key you're playing. And unless you practice playing them keys, and you don't practice as much playing those keys as you would, and a more easier key such as B flat, E flat, F, C natural, even G. You understand what I'm talking about? But most of the stuff is there. Now Fletcher Henderson, a lot of guys complained about his music because he said that the sharp was beautiful, you know, it was more beautiful than the flats. So a lot of his stuff, I read some of his music, a lot of his stuff was in E and D and C sharp and like that, see what I'm talking about? But there's a general rule that I was going to play the blues, the guy coming right now and said I'm going to play, he'll play the blues even B flat or E flat. Either one of those keys. He won't take the C sharp. Well Rene, Rene was stout, he was a little small. See, he and Buddy Petit was around the same size. I heard Buddy, but I didn't know who he was. Now I actually said about, especially the fellas from downtown, say that Rene was better than Louis Armstrong. But I don't agree with him. First thing, Louis' range was greater. And I'd go to say that his tone was more beautiful. Louis Armstrong had a beautiful tone. And Louis Armstrong, we were at the Surviving Garden right there and we had Chloe. Chloe's in D flat. He comes right back to what I was saying. Now, it's tunes I can play very well, you know, our solos, our solos, in D flat. And it's some team tunes that are warming too. So it's Chloe, he passed out the music. He had a photograph in mind when I'm coming to it. And we played it, we played the music down, then he began to pass out the solos. Well we wasn't used to playing that. Well Stardust is D flat, you know, and we played Stardust and like that. But this Chloe, da da da da da da da da da da da da da da. He played in C down there. Yeah, well D flat. So well you know, he'd play a tune down once and turn the music over and play it right down like he was looking at the music. So all of us fell down by the wayside but him. That man played one of the prettiest solos on that Chloe that ever heard. And falling in love and things like that. Ding dong daddy. All them things back in there you know. He was really playing there you know. But later on he became a commercial you know. And that's where he made his money. See all that pretty stuff he was making and running things. The public is, don't understand jazz music as well as they should. They don't know where the fellas are making you know what I'm talking about. But they say that, see the boy that died in 31 was down here, buddy, I suppose over ate him, some people say ate himself to death. I wouldn't say that because I don't know that. It was alleged that he did that you know. So that makes it better for me. But he wasn't very strong. No, he was like Mud Carrier. Mud Carrier wasn't. Now Mud Carrier made Joe throw his horn away one day. Really? Yeah, Mud Carrier. Well Mud Carrier would take a glass, an ordinary glass like that and get a lot of sounds out of it just like Joe Oliver. But he was low like George Mitchell. You ever heard of George Mitchell when Joe was wrong? He wasn't very strong. You understand? And he'd get out on that low register there and run you crazy. So Joe said. You mean I would play Joe? Oh yeah, well Joe would stop me pawn chopping and get in my horn. And he said, well he can use your enjoyment. And he couldn't much worry to death. Now Willie Hightower was sweet jazz. You ever hear his play? Yeah, on record. Sweet, yeah. He used to be sweet. Played the blues. Yeah, sweet.
How was Punch Miller?

Well Punch Miller, he made a lot of stuff. Yeah, he made a lot of his runs and arpeggios and things like that. And you see poor Punch here. We used to play concerts quite often in Chicago. And Punch used to, you know, too much, too much. Played with him in the 20's?
Huh? Did you play with him in the 20's? Yeah.
Yeah, in the early 30's too. Was he like that then too?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. He had the power, he was good in those days.
Yeah, guy carried it too. All the time, yeah.
But what did you think about it? You said that René used to play the blues in these ladies?

Well René played in C Sharp. You mean C Sharp. C Sharp. Well that's the same thing. I sat in there with that, I grabbed the trumbo one night, Morrissey here and played with him. And I was feeling around him, you know. You were trying to find the trumbo? Feeling all around, trying to find the key. It was damn near old when I found the key, you understand what I'm talking about. Because I hadn't been used to playing.
Did you think René was a very good trumbo player?

Oh, I know he was. It was too bad he didn't do any recording them out there, and Buddy too. Buddy was on the art of Bunk. Now I played with Bunk in Chicago. Oh yeah? Yeah, Bunk, the central Bunk. The later years in the 40's now. Yeah, Bunk came up, but I could still see why they were talking about he was so great and he had taught Lil Armstrong during that time. But Bunk, every train they went there, they went to the station looking for Bunk to arrive, and he wouldn't be on that train. Finally, about the fourth train, the other Bunk, and they don't have no horn.
The horn might be on another train.

See they rediscovered him from New Ile Berry. He was in New Ile Berry, they were working. And so Bunk played that night, and George Brunus was there, and Paul Morales, and we had Brother McGrummers on the piano, and Lee Collins, he used Lee Collins on. We had Darnell Howard, and somebody else.
What did you think about Bunk playing then?
Well I could tell he wasn't very strong, but I could see why they raved over him.
Did you know him down here?
I saw him.
But you never heard him play then?

I saw him and heard him play when I was a kid. I didn't know who he was, because I wasn't interested. All I cared during that time was to dance and follow the band. That's all I cared. You didn't know the names, man. No, I didn't know the names. I heard Buddy. Player Buddy was just starting out. The first time I heard Armstrong, the dedication of the Tonlefong Playground, they had a little band to come out and play. And they had a fellow named Frazier playing the baritone. I know two or three guys. Rene was back there with him too.
Do you think Rene was like a good reader and all that too? I don't think so. His band was just ad libbing when you heard him.

Well, that's all the whole band was doing. Yeah, they weren't using music at all. Yeah, that's all they was doing. And Lee Collins told me a tale about Rene. He says one day, they were advertising the band, and he saw Louie and Louie came on and got on the wagon. He said, dude, those days it was a wagon. And they always carried a thick rope or chain. See those guys, people would take them lock the wagons together with these chains. And they couldn't get away. They just had to take it if it was better than you, see. And so they saw Rene about two blocks away with his band. And so Rene at the same time saw Lee. But Louie was hiding down in the truck, in the wagon, see. And so they came together and he gave Louie his horn and they had quite a battle there. Rene was small but he was stout. He played a lot upstairs you know. But he wasn't as strong as Louie Armstrong. He wasn't as strong as Louie Armstrong, but he was strong, much stronger than Buddy Petit. Now Buddy Petit played a whole lot of pretty stuff down in the low range. And so Louie and I were with him, we started making the 300 high Cs and in the Tiger rag, you know, in the every morning high F. We played in New York and we broke it up. We played in Boston against Fletcher Anderson, the band. And after he did that, that was it. 300, we counted. And so many courses, Tiger rag and like that. They had a lip. Yeah, oh yeah. He just batted his lip up. He had a lot of trouble. Louie had a lot of trouble, period. Here we had, he used to come out, you wouldn't let him come around until 6 o'clock. And I never saw so many cousins in my whole life. And they'd have a line about from here to, oh, longer from here to in front of his house. On both sides, he'd come out. He'd get well first to first meet. He never refused. Just like I have a, I intend to bring it, I had a right up in the Times. Sometimes you could hold my picture. Louie's a little inset right on the side. And I stated that I was with Louie Armstrong and how he fed and put shoes on my feet, which he did. During the operation after Louie disbanded his band, I was selling ads for the union. There was a little kid he called Lil Jon, a great little drummer. And something was wrong with his spine, so he was giving this benefit for his medical bills, you know. And so I met Louie and I was in bad shape. One of my shoes, the sole was loose, you know, I had it tied with a string. Every time I walked, go flip. Well I had my daughter and my mother take it, see what I'm talking about? So every time I walked, flip flop, flip flop, flip flop. So I had a string tied around. So I met him 39 South Park. He said, hey Nosey. I said, hey Dip. So he came, I said Dip, take one of these ads for me. He's taking a $20 ad and he gave me $20. Well that's the type of fellow he was. That's the type of fellow he was. So I spoke about it.
Why'd they call you Nosey? I don't call him my nose. Where did you put it? Huh? Where did you put your nose?
Where did I put it? Well I didn't put it anywhere.
You didn't stick your nose in other people's business.
Well I have done some of that too. I guess everybody sometimes knows to stick your nose in other people's business.
Well you always wanted to know. Yeah.

Well I tried to, the point that I was trying to rob, I was trying to learn. And I thought the best way to learn was to listen to people that played better than you. You can't learn anything from a fellow that don't play as much as you can.
Oh let me ask you something. When was it you came back to Nosey and how long did you stay?
Well after 21, then I came back in 31.
No but the first time you came back you said that's before you even started really playing music.

Well I was, I was in 21. Yeah what made you come back then? Well I came back on a visit. Oh I see. My aunt at that time was living there I think around Steya and Saratoga or something along there. So I came back. You stayed a good while? Yeah I stayed about a month. Oh I see. Yeah just about a month. Then I went and they kept writing to me and come on we got some jobs and things like that. That's when you were just getting into it? Yeah but I didn't, during that month I didn't play. I just sat in with the. You went around and saw the fellow. Yeah. Yeah.
But how old were you about when you started playing jobs in around Chicago?

Oh I started playing about, I was playing pretty good in eight months. You were about 19 or something like that? I always did get a fair tone you know. It was a Mexican show, just a solid tone. Yeah. And so then I, then they formed a band. There's two Simeon brothers which is from New Orleans. Yeah. And there was Jimmy Mackenzie on the drum, myself and Bernie and sometimes Dominic. And so Richard Jones on piano, one time he had the band.
So you started working pretty fast after you.
Yeah I didn't let no grass grow my feet. No. No I started. But did you become a professional musician?
Huh? You started becoming a professional musician.

Yeah well the guys would call me Ham. You see when they think you didn't play so well they call you Ham. Yeah right. And so I was determined to make some of those guys eat the woods which I did. Jack, why don't you hunt them fish? I said, I believe I will, Joe. So Joe carried me to this market. There's three of them. I'm going to put them in one direction, one here and one diagonal and one in the next corner on Fulton Street. A guy gave me 280 pounds of fish for seventeen dollars. So I'd already been to the market. I bought me some tomatoes and lettuce and things to go with these fish. It was on a Friday. And so on the way back to the garage, that fish began to hit me in the nose, you know? I said, my uncle's name was Cookie. I said, Cookie? I said, you smell what I smell? He said, you're damn right. He said, look like we got some rotten fish. I said, oh boy. I said, it must be rotten. I said, mm-hmm. So we went off the garage and we was pondering what to do with the fish. I hate to lose my seventeen dollars and don't have a load either. It's too late for me to go pick up a load at the market. So I said, well, I'll just reimburse the people as they catch me tomorrow. Saturday's my best day. So we had a tub of water, warm water. We had soap. We had steel and good knives and clean towels and everything. I sold $22 away from fish before I moved from the garage. And I didn't want to sell those people. It was my neighbors. I didn't want to sell them any, but I had to come to the garage. So I said, oh Lord, I'm dead. So we made our rounds and sold all that fish. But I still could smell that fish. So the next day around, the people said, oh my goodness, Mr. Jackson. Where'd you get that nice fish? I said, well, I'll go now. So anyhow, I wouldn't go back to the same bar and buy a fish. I knew I'd say today that that fish was rotten. I wouldn't go back to him. I went to another place. I got Lake Superior. I got push. I got catfish. It was high. Catfish was about 80 cents a pound then, see. And Joe went back and got 400 some pounds of fish. He had two trucks. And he bought 400 pounds and had to give the people the money back. Yeah. I'd lose all these customers. How did you make out in the 50s with Natty Dominic and Baby and Baby and Baby? Yeah. Or lose all these customers.
